nameStory: The Hudsonian Whimbrel gets its name from Hudson Bay, the vast subarctic waters where these birds breed across northern Canada. The word 'whimbrel' comes from their haunting, whistled calls that sound like 'whim-whim-whim' echoing across coastal mudflats. This smaller cousin of the curlew shares the same curved bill design but earned its own name for its distinctive size and northern breeding grounds.
description: The Hudsonian Whimbrel is a medium-sized shorebird with a gracefully curved bill that looks like a miniature version of its larger curlew cousins. About the size of a crow, it sports mottled brown and buff plumage that helps it blend into coastal environments. Its most striking feature is that long, downward-curving bill, perfectly designed for probing deep into mud and sand for hidden prey. These elegant waders are among the most far-traveling shorebirds, covering thousands of miles during migration.

idTips.label: Curved Bill
idTips.description: Long, thin bill curves distinctly downward like a gentle arc - not as dramatically curved as larger curlews but unmistakably bent. The bill feels firm and pointed when observed closely, perfect for probing soft substrates.

idTips.label: Head Stripes
idTips.description: Bold dark stripes run through the eye with lighter stripes above and below, creating a distinctive striped pattern on the head that stands out even at a distance.

idTips.label: Mottled Plumage
idTips.description: Overall brown and buff coloring with intricate mottling and streaking throughout - appears richly textured rather than plain, like a well-worn leather jacket with natural patterns.

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than the massive Long-billed Curlew but larger than most other shorebirds - roughly crow-sized with long legs that give it an elegant, stretched appearance when walking.

idTips.label: Flight Call
idTips.description: Distinctive series of liquid whistles that sound like 'whim-whim-whim' or 'pip-pip-pip-pip' - once heard, this musical call becomes unmistakable and carries well across open areas.

habitat: Look for Hudsonian Whimbrels along New England's coastal areas, especially mudflats, salt marshes, and rocky shorelines during migration periods. They favor areas where retreating tides expose rich feeding grounds full of marine worms, crabs, and mollusks. You might also spot them in nearby coastal fields and short-grass areas where they hunt for terrestrial prey.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs from late April through May as birds head north to breeding grounds. Watch for small flocks along the coast, often mixed with other migrating shorebirds.
seasonality.summer: Only occasional non-breeding birds remain in New England during summer months. Most adults are on Arctic breeding grounds raising young.
seasonality.fall: Best viewing season runs from July through September as adults and juveniles migrate south. Fall birds may linger longer than spring migrants, offering better observation opportunities.
seasonality.winter: Very rare in New England winters - most birds continue south to warmer coastal areas from the Carolinas to South America.

funFact: Hudsonian Whimbrels are incredible navigators that can fly non-stop for over 2,500 miles during migration, using their ability to sense magnetic fields and even infrasound from ocean waves to guide them across vast stretches of open ocean without any landmarks.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Long-billed Curlew, but whimbrels are noticeably smaller with a less dramatically curved bill and bold head stripes that curlews lack. Remember: whimbrels wear racing stripes on their heads, curlews have plain faces and much longer, more curved bills.
contextualKnowledge: The Hudsonian Whimbrel is sometimes called the Hudsonian Curlew in older field guides, which can cause confusion since it's actually a different species from true curlews. Recent studies suggest there may be subspecies differences, but for New England birders, any whimbrel you see will likely be this Hudsonian form.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Eurasian Whimbrel, the Hudsonian Whimbrel has a slightly warmer, more buffy tone to its plumage and subtly different head stripe patterns. In New England, you're much more likely to encounter the Hudsonian form, as Eurasian Whimbrels are rare vagrants. Both species are smaller and more delicately built than the massive Long-billed Curlew, with proportionally shorter, less extremely curved bills.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Hudsonian Whimbrel, the Eurasian shows warmer brown and rufous tones rather than the grayer appearance of the Hudsonian.
